Two methods for 3D printing fibers are proposed: the fiber bridging method and the extrude-and-pull method.
Both methods can produce fibers with aspect ratios (length-to-thickness ratio) greater than 100.
The fiber bridging method results in thicker fibers on average compared to the extrude-and-pull method.
Decreasing the horizontal or vertical separation between fibers increases the sound absorption, especially at lower frequencies.
Increasing the extruder travel rate for the bridging method produces thinner fibers and lower sound absorption.
For the extrude-and-pull method, the fibers are thickest near the extrusion location and the thickness gradually decreases along the length.
The dominant absorption mechanism for the 3D printed fibrous absorbers is the dissipation of incident acoustic energy through visco-inertial and thermal losses.
The sound absorption behavior of the 3D printed fibrous absorbers is modeled using the Johnson-Champoux-Allard (JCA) semi-empirical analytical model.
The 3D printed fibrous absorbers provide good sound absorption performance in the medium-to-high frequency range, typically between 1000-6000 Hz.
Previous research on 3D printed porous sound absorbers has focused on fabricating foams, lattices, and perforated panels, but not fibrous absorbers.
Potential applications for the 3D printed fibrous sound absorbers include aeronautics, computer server design, automotive engineering, and automatic hand dryer manufacturing.
The average printing time for the fiber bridging method was 90 minutes, while for the extrude-and-pull method it was 110 minutes.
The fiber bridging method sometimes resulted in fiber bending due to heat from the extruder warping adjacent fibers.
For the extrude-and-pull method, too small extrusion amounts resulted in unformed, under-extruded fibers, while over-extrusion left globs of filament behind each fiber.
Changing the inter-layer angle did not result in any appreciable change in the sound absorption performance for the bridging method.
